Based on the STAC specification documentation, here are the **required fields of a STAC Item**:

A STAC Item is a **GeoJSON Feature** with additional STAC-specific foreign members. Its required fields come from two sources:

---

### 🔷 Fields Inherited from GeoJSON
| Field Name   | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | Must be `"Feature"` (as required by GeoJSON). |
| `geometry` | GeoJSON Geometry \| null | The spatial footprint of the Item (e.g., a Polygon). Can be `null` if the item has no geometry. |
| `bbox` | array of numbers | Bounding box of the geometry: `[west, south, east, north]`. Required when `geometry` is not `null`. |
| `properties` | object | A dictionary of metadata about the Item. Must contain at least the **`datetime`** field (a UTC datetime string, or `null` if `start_datetime`/`end_datetime` are used instead). |

---

### 🔷 STAC-Specific Required Fields
| Field Name        | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `stac_version`    | string | The STAC specification version the Item follows (e.g., `"1.0.0"`). |
| `id`              | string | A unique identifier for the Item within the Catalog/Collection. |
| `links`           | array of Link objects | A list of references to related resources (e.g., to its parent Catalog or Collection, and a `self` link). |
| `assets`          | Map\<string, Asset\> | A dictionary of downloadable or streamable assets associated with the Item (e.g., imagery files). Each key is a unique asset identifier. |

---

### 🔷 Optional but Notable
- **`stac_extensions`** – an array of URIs identifying any STAC extensions used; not strictly required but strongly recommended when extensions are applied.
- **`collection`**– the ID of the Collection this Item belongs to; recommended when the Item is part of a Collection.

---

### Summary
In short, a valid STAC Item **must** have:
`type`, `stac_version`, `id`, `geometry`, `bbox`, `properties` (with `datetime`), `links`, and `assets`.

These fields collectively ensure an Item is both valid GeoJSON and a self-describing, discoverable spatiotemporal asset record.

Great — here is a clear breakdown of the differences between a **STAC Catalog** and a **STAC Collection**, grounded in the specification:

---

## STAC Catalog vs. STAC Collection

### 🗂️ STAC Catalog — The Structural Backbone
A **Catalog** is the fundamental building block for organizing and linking STAC content. Its purpose is **discovery**: it provides a simple, recursive linking structure that groups Items and other Catalogs together so they can be browsed by humans or crawled by machines.

**Required fields:**
| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | Must be `"Catalog"` |
| `id` | Unique identifier |
| `description` | Human-readable description |
| `stac_version` | STAC version implemented |
| `links` | Links to child Catalogs, Collections, or Items |

A Catalog makes **no formal distinction** between a root and child catalog — it's purely about structure and navigation.

---

### 📦 STAC Collection — A Catalog with Richer Metadata
A **Collection** is a **superset of a Catalog**. It includes all four required Catalog fields and adds extra fields to describe the *dataset* as a whole. Because of this, **every valid Collection is also a valid Catalog**, but not vice versa.

**Additional required fields (beyond Catalog):**
| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `type` | Must be `"Collection"` (not `"Catalog"`) |
| `license` | Data license (e.g., `"proprietary"`, `"CC-BY-4.0"`) |
| `extent` | Spatial and temporal extent of the contained Items |

Collections also typically carry many **optional but common fields** such as `title`, `providers`, `summaries`, `assets`, and links to fuller external metadata (e.g., ISO 19115).

---

### Key Differences at a Glance

| Feature | Catalog | Collection |
|---|---|---|
| Structural linking | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes (inherits all Catalog fields) |
| `license` field | ❌ No | ✅ Required |
| `extent` field | ❌ No | ✅ Required |
| `type` value | `"Catalog"` | `"Collection"` |
| Describes a dataset | ❌ Minimal | ✅ Yes, with rich metadata |
| Is also a valid Catalog? | ✅ Yes | ✅ Yes |

---

### In Summary
Think of a **Catalog** as a *folder* — it organizes and links things together. A **Collection** is a *labelled, described folder* — it does everything a Catalog does, but also carries meaningful metadata (spatial/temporal extent, license, etc.) to describe the group of Items it contains as a coherent dataset.

According to the STAC specification, a **STAC Item** should use the following media type:

> ### `application/geo+json`

This is because a STAC Item is a **GeoJSON file** (conforming to [RFC 7946](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7946)), and the appropriate media type for GeoJSON is `application/geo+json`, as defined in [RFC 7946 §12](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7946#section-12).

For reference, here's how that compares to the other core STAC object types:

| STAC Object | Media Type |
|---|---|
| **Item** | `application/geo+json` |
| **Collection** | `application/json` |
| **Catalog** | `application/json` |

Items get the more specific `application/geo+json` type because they are GeoJSON Features with a geometry, while Catalogs and Collections are plain JSON documents.

## Standalone Collection

A **standalone Collection** is a STAC Collection that **does not link to any Items**.

Here are the key points about it, drawn directly from the STAC specification:

- **Definition:** It is simply a STAC Collection with no child Item links — it describes a dataset at a high level without pointing to individual spatiotemporal assets.

- **Extended Metadata via Summaries:** Since a standalone Collection has no Items to carry metadata fields, it is permitted to **reuse Item-level extension fields inside the `summaries` field** of the Collection to provide richer description. For example:
  - Fields like `platform` or `proj:code` make good candidates, as they are often the same for the entire Collection.
  - Fields like `eo:cloud_cover` are less suitable, since they typically vary heavily across scenes.

- **Provider Discretion:** The data provider is free to decide which Item-level fields are meaningful to include in `summaries` for a standalone Collection.

In essence, a standalone Collection acts as a self-contained metadata record for a dataset — useful when you want to describe a collection of data without (yet) exposing or linking individual scenes/assets.

Here is a full breakdown of the `extent` field in a STAC Collection, based on the specification documentation:

---

## The `extent` Field in a STAC Collection

The `extent` field (also referred to as the **Extent Object**) describes the **spatio-temporal extents** of a Collection — i.e., *where* and *when* the data it contains was acquired. Both sub-fields are **required**.

It is composed of two required child objects:

---

### 1. `spatial` — Spatial Extent Object

- Contains a **`bbox`** field: an array of bounding boxes, each expressed as an array of numbers in **WGS 84 longitude/latitude**.
- Bounding boxes can be **2D** (`[west, south, east, north]`) or **3D** (adding min/max elevation in meters).
- The **first bounding box** always represents the **overall spatial extent** of the collection.
- Additional bounding boxes can be provided to describe more precise sub-regions or clusters of data.

> Example (whole Earth): `[[-180.0, -90.0, 180.0, 90.0]]`
> Example (with elevation): `[[-180.0, -90.0, -100.0, 180.0, 90.0, 150.0]]`

---

### 2. `temporal` — Temporal Extent Object

- Contains an **`interval`** field: an array of date/time intervals, where each interval is a two-element array of timestamps (start and end).
- Timestamps follow the RFC 3339 format.
- Either the start or end can be **`null`** to represent an open-ended interval (e.g., ongoing collections have a `null` end time).

---

### Summary

| Element    | Type                     | Required | Description                                              |
|------------|--------------------------|----------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `spatial`  | Spatial Extent Object    | ✅ Yes   | Bounding box(es) covering the collection's spatial reach |
| `temporal` | Temporal Extent Object   | ✅ Yes   | Time interval(s) covering the collection's temporal reach|

In short, the `extent` field gives users a quick, high-level understanding of the geographic area and time period that a Collection covers, without having to inspect individual Items.

Based on the STAC specification documentation, a valid STAC Catalog requires the following **required fields**:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | Must be set to `"Catalog"` (to identify the object type) |
| `stac_version` | string | The version of the STAC specification that the Catalog implements (e.g., `"1.0.0"`) |
| `id` | string | A unique identifier for the Catalog |
| `description` | string | A human-readable description of the Catalog |
| `links` | array | A list of references to other documents/resources (used for browsing and crawling) |

> *Any JSON object that contains all the required fields is a valid STAC Catalog object.*

A few additional notes:
- **`stac_extensions`** (a list of extension identifiers) is optional but commonly included.
- A **STAC Collection** is also a valid Catalog — it contains all four core Catalog fields (`id`, `description`, `stac_version`, and `links`) and adds a few more required fields (`license` and `extent`).
- The required fields are intentionally minimal to keep the spec flexible and easy to implement.

Based on the official STAC specification documentation, here is a thorough explanation of the `assets` field in a STAC Item:

---

## The `assets` Field in a STAC Item

### What it is
The `assets` property is a **dictionary (map) of Asset Objects**, each identified by a **unique string key** (e.g., `"B02"`, `"thumbnail"`, `"metadata"`). Every asset refers to data associated with the Item that can be **downloaded or streamed**.

---

### What Each Asset Object Contains

Each Asset Object in the dictionary is expected to include the following fields:

| Field | Required? | Description |
|-------|-----------|-------------|
| `href` | **Required** | The URI/URL to the actual file (direct download or streaming link) |
| `type` | Recommended | The media type (MIME type) of the file (e.g., `image/tiff`, `application/json`) |
| `title` | Recommended | A human-readable name for the asset |
| `description` | Optional | A longer description of what the asset contains |
| `roles` | Recommended | A list of semantic roles describing the asset's purpose (see below) |

---

### What Should Be Included

Assets in a STAC Item should cover:
- The **main data file(s)** (e.g., imagery bands)
- Any **"sidecar" files** that help a client interpret the data, such as:
  - Extended metadata (XML, JSON, etc.)
  - Unusable data masks
  - Satellite ephemeris data

For datasets like Landsat that span multiple files, **all files should be linked**.

---

### Recommended Roles

The spec strongly recommends including at least:
- A **thumbnail** asset (with `"roles": ["thumbnail"]`) for quick visual preview
- One or more **data** assets (with `"roles": ["data"]`) for the actual science data

---

### Example (conceptual)
```json
"assets": {
  "thumbnail": {
    "href": "https://example.com/scene_thumb.jpg",
    "type": "image/jpeg",
    "title": "Preview Image",
    "roles": ["thumbnail"]
  },
  "B04": {
    "href": "https://example.com/scene_B04.tif",
    "type": "image/tiff; application=geotiff",
    "title": "Red Band",
    "roles": ["data"]
  },
  "metadata": {
    "href": "https://example.com/scene_metadata.xml",
    "type": "application/xml",
    "title": "Scene Metadata",
    "roles": ["metadata"]
  }
}
```

---

**In summary**, the `assets` field is the heart of a STAC Item — it is the dictionary that maps human-friendly keys to the actual downloadable or streamable files, along with descriptive metadata to help clients understand and use those files. *(Source: stac-spec-core — Item fields, Assets section)*

Here is a comprehensive explanation of how STAC extensions work, grounded in the specification documentation:

---

## How STAC Extensions Work

### 1. Purpose
STAC's core specification intentionally covers only the most universal metadata fields. **Extensions** are the mechanism for adding domain-specific or use-case-specific fields and behaviours on top of that core — for example, fields describing satellite view angles, EO band information, or data processing provenance.

---

### 2. Scope
Each extension declares which STAC objects it applies to. An extension may extend:
- **Items** (the most common)
- **Collections**
- **Catalogs**
- Any combination of the above

An object must **only** declare extensions that directly apply to itself. For example, a Catalog must not list extensions that are only used in its child Items or Collections.

---

### 3. Declaration via `stac_extensions`
Every STAC object (Item, Collection, Catalog) has a `stac_extensions` field — a **list of URLs pointing to JSON Schema files** for each extension the object implements. For example:

```json
{
  "stac_version": "1.0.0",
  "stac_extensions": [
    "https://stac-extensions.github.io/eo/v1.1.0/schema.json",
    "https://stac-extensions.github.io/view/v1.0.0/schema.json"
  ],
  ...
}
```

These URLs serve two purposes:
- **Identification**: they uniquely identify which extension is being used (and at which version).
- **Validation**: the URLs point to JSON Schema files that can be used by validation tools to check the object's compliance with the extension.

---

### 4. Field Naming Conventions (Prefixes)
Extensions add new fields, and to avoid naming conflicts they follow a **prefix convention**. Related fields share a common prefix (a short namespace), separated from the field name by a colon. For example:
- `view:azimuth`, `view:off_nadir` — from the View Geometry extension
- `eo:bands`, `eo:cloud_cover` — from the EO (Electro-Optical) extension

This keeps fields organised and avoids collisions between different extensions or with the core spec.

---

### 5. JSON Schema & Validation
The core STAC specification itself is described with **JSON Schema**, and extensions follow the same pattern. Each extension ships its own JSON Schema file (hosted at the URL listed in `stac_extensions`). Validation tools can fetch those schemas and verify that an Item, Collection, or Catalog correctly implements the extension.

---

### 6. Custom & Community Extensions
- **Community extensions** are maintained at [stac-extensions.github.io](https://stac-extensions.github.io), which serves as the central registry.
- **Custom extensions** are also permitted — any implementer can define their own fields. The recommendation is to still use the prefix convention and provide a JSON Schema for interoperability.

---

### Summary Table

| Aspect | Details |
|---|---|
| **Where declared** | `stac_extensions` field (list of schema URLs) |
| **Applies to** | Items, Collections, and/or Catalogs (per extension's scope) |
| **Field convention** | `prefix:fieldname` (e.g., `eo:bands`) |
| **Validation** | Via JSON Schema files pointed to by the extension URLs |
| **Registry** | https://stac-extensions.github.io |

Extensions make STAC highly flexible while keeping the core simple and universal. The URL-as-identifier approach means extensions are self-describing and version-pinned, making interoperability straightforward.

## What is a SpatioTemporal Asset in STAC?

According to the official STAC specification, a **SpatioTemporal Asset** is defined as:

> *"Any file that represents information about the Earth captured in a certain space and time."*

### Key Characteristics

- It is **spatially bounded** (tied to a specific geographic location) and **temporally bounded** (captured at a specific time or time range).
- It is the **actual data file** being referenced — not the GeoJSON metadata itself. The GeoJSON (a STAC Item) serves as an **index** pointing *to* the asset.

### Examples of SpatioTemporal Assets

| Type | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Imagery** | Satellite, aerial, drone imagery |
| **SAR** | Synthetic Aperture Radar data |
| **Point Clouds** | LiDAR, Structure from Motion (SfM) |
| **Data Cubes** | Multi-dimensional analysis-ready datasets |
| **Full Motion Video** | Time-series video captures of Earth |
| **Derived Data** | Products derived from any of the above |

### What It Is NOT

Traditional **vector data layers** (e.g., shapefiles, GeoPackages) are **not recommended** to be represented as SpatioTemporal Assets, as they don't conceptually fit the model.

### How It Fits in STAC

A STAC **Item** is the core object that *describes* a SpatioTemporal Asset. It is a GeoJSON Feature that includes:
- The **geometry** (location on Earth)
- The **time** the asset represents
- **Links to the actual asset files** (for direct download or streaming)
- A **thumbnail** for quick browsing

In short, the asset is the *data*, and the STAC Item is the *metadata record* that makes that data discoverable and accessible.

## 1. What does STAC call a "scene"?

STAC calls it an **Item**. According to the specification:

> *"A STAC Item object represents a unit of data and metadata, typically representing a **single scene of data at one place and time**."*

An Item is a **GeoJSON Feature** augmented with spatio-temporal metadata — including the time the asset represents, a thumbnail, and links to the actual data assets (e.g., satellite bands). Items are the core objects in a STAC Catalog or Collection.
